Synchronised stereo photos and videos with Android phones
For Google Pixel 7a, Pixel 4 and Xreal Beam Pro

SyncCamPhone turns two (or more) Android phones into one stereo camera. One phone is the CONTROL phone: you operate everything from it. The other phones are camera phones: they follow the CONTROL phone. All phones take each photo, and record each video frame, at the same moment. The left and right pictures can then be combined into a 3D photo or video with stereo software.

The phones agree on a common clock over Wi-Fi. For video, every camera keeps its frames in step with the others. For photos, every phone uses the camera frame closest to the same moment. Typical differences between the phones are a few hundredths of a millisecond.
Stereo photos: JPEG, RAW (DNG) or both, with the same exposure, white balance and focus on all phones.
HDR photos: a short burst of frames merged into one photo with more detail in the bright and dark parts. In dark scenes, extra frames are averaged automatically (Night).
Astro: a series of long exposures (up to 16 s per frame) on a tripod for night skies and night landscapes.
Time-lapse: synchronised stereo photos at a fixed interval.
Stereo video up to 4K at 30 frames per second, with sound.
Lenses: main, ultra-wide and front camera, chosen on the CONTROL phone.
MONO: the same photo and video modes on a single phone.
Remote trigger (experimental): presses the shutter of Google Camera or the record button of Blackmagic Camera on all phones at the same moment.

Two phones of the same model: Google Pixel 7a (recommended), Pixel 4, or Xreal Beam Pro (its left lens). Other phones: the app finds their lenses by itself; Probe → Timing test shows whether a phone can be synchronised.
A stereo bar or rig that holds both phones side by side, in landscape, at the same height.
For Astro and time-lapse: a stable tripod.
Wi-Fi: the CONTROL phone opens a hotspot and the camera phones connect to it. No internet is needed.
Use two phones of the same model and the same app version (shown on the start screen). Different phone models have different lenses and timing and do not give good stereo pairs.

All phones must be on the same Wi-Fi network. A camera phone on another network keeps switching its camera on and off (the picture flickers). Do not run a second CONTROL phone on the same network.
A house Wi-Fi also works, but the hotspot of the CONTROL phone gives the most stable clock sync. If another phone opens the hotspot, all messages pass through it and the sync gets less precise.

After CONTROL + CAMERA or CAMERA the app asks for the position of this camera: LEFT or RIGHT. Seen from behind the phones, the left phone writes files ending in -l, the right phone files ending in -r. Stereo software pairs the files by these endings.

If two phones choose the same side, a red note on the CONTROL phone and on those cameras names them for a few seconds ("Both RIGHT: … the file names will not pair"). It is only a warning: a third camera may share a side on purpose.
Once the roles are chosen, the cameras start by themselves. Wait until the status at the top left turns green (SYNC, see chapter 3). This takes about 20–40 s after the start.
Hold the phones in landscape. Everything is operated from the CONTROL phone; the camera phones show their own picture and status.

After a time without use (120 s by default, see SYSTEM settings) or with the moon button, all cameras switch off. The CONTROL phone shows tap to wake, the camera phones tap the CONTROL phone to wake. After waking, the exposure is measured again automatically.

Keep SyncCamPhone in front on the CONTROL phone. If its screen goes off or another app is opened, it stops answering; the cameras reconnect when it is back, and the clock needs about 30 s to settle again.

5.3 JPEG and RAW: shutter time and Night
JPEG, RAW and RAW+JPEG are single photos, processed by the camera itself (natural skin and detail). Three settings in Settings → PHOTO (shown only for these formats) decide how they are exposed:
Slowest shutter (default 1/31 s) and Max ISO (default 800): the limits of AE. For people who talk or move, 1/60 s or 1/125 s keeps them sharp.

When the light is short at these limits, AE says so in a yellow note (e.g. Not enough light: -1.3 EV at 1/31 s ISO 800) and the exposure chip shows -1.3 EV. Brighten the picture with the brightness slider that opens after AE, or with the ISO slider: both may go beyond the limits, up to ISO 3200 (the next AE returns to the limits). Or raise Max ISO / Slowest shutter and press AE again.

Night (default off): when on and the light is short, the app takes several frames right around the moment of the press and averages them; the photo chip shows · Night and the photo takes a few seconds. Moving parts (a talking mouth, hands) are taken from one frame only, so they stay sharp. Night photos have their own gentle look: the Local contrast and Sharpening settings do not apply to them.
In dim light, Night gives less noise and more detail than a single JPEG, also for people. For fast movement use JPEG with a shorter Slowest shutter.

HDR takes a short burst. The phones need to stay still for about a second, and moving objects may look blurred or be taken from one frame only. The merging takes a few seconds after the burst; the next photo can be taken when the shutter is ready again.

Extra frames (up to) limits how much brighter the longest frame may be: 1 = mild (3 EV), 3 = full range (9 EV). The HDR & ASTRO tab sets the maximum ISO, the slowest shutter time, Movement (sharp or natural blur) and Brightness of the result (night look, natural, bright).
In very dark scenes, more frames are averaged (up to 15). Hold the phones as still as possible or use a tripod.
Astro selected: the photo chip shows Astro (1), the exposure chip the planned frames (2), the shutter ASTRO #N in yellow (3).
Put the phones on a tripod. They must not move during the whole series.
Select Format → Astro and tap AE. The chips show the planned exposures.
Press the shutter (ASTRO #N). The series starts on all phones at the same moment about 4–5 s later, so that touching the phone does not shake the first frame.
Do not touch the phones until the series has ended (1 or 2 minutes, see HDR & ASTRO settings). During the series the shutter shows STOP ASTRO: press it to cancel.
The phones merge the frames (some seconds) and save the photo.
The final picture is made from the longest frames, like a real long exposure: lamps are white, and moving lights (cars, planes) leave trails. A series has at most 16 frames.
Astro is never remembered: when the app is started again, the format returns to HDR. This prevents starting a long series by mistake.

Settings → PHOTO → Time-lapse: On, the interval in seconds and the number of frames (0 = until stopped). The shutter then shows TIME-LAPSE (blue); press it to start, during the series it shows STOP n/N.
Every shot is a normal synchronised photo in the chosen format (not Astro).
Focus and white balance are locked at the start on all phones.
Time-lapse AE: locked at start for constant light; each shot (smoothed) measures about 3 s before every photo and changes the exposure by at most 1/3 EV per shot (e.g. a sunrise without flicker).
Each series goes into its own folder Timelapse_NNNN (NNNN = number of its first photo) on every phone. No standby during a series.
Choose an interval longer than one shot takes: JPEG about 2 s, HDR and Night bursts 8 s or more. Otherwise shots are delayed.
Choose MONO camera on the start screen to use all photo and video modes on one phone. The status shows ● MONO; files are saved in the Mono folder.
The AE chip measures the scene once and gives all phones the same exposure. It does not keep changing it, so both pictures of a pair always match. Measure again when the light changes.
Brightness panel: after pressing AE, or with a long press on AE (photo and video).
Reference brightness: moves the measured exposure from -3 to +3 EV (above the frame time, ISO is raised instead).

Shutter / Clipped %: chooses what the slider changes. Clipped % sets how much of the picture may be overexposed (0 to 10 %) and measures again. Small values protect bright parts (a lamp in the picture makes the rest darker); larger values give a brighter picture where small lights may burn out.
The panel appears only when you press AE, not after the automatic measurement at the start or after standby.
Resolution, frame rate (29.8 → 30 fps: see below) and bit rate. Tap it to open the video settings.
Starts the recording on all phones; press again to stop. The top bar shows ● REC and the recording time.

The phones record at 29.8 frames per second: slightly below 30, so that the app can keep the frames of all phones in step. With Conform to 30 fps (default on) the file is marked as 30 fps; it plays 0.7 % faster, which is not noticeable. Both files have exactly the same frames, so they can be put side by side without searching for the start.

Bitrate mode (VIDEO settings): VBR is an average target - the encoder uses less in easy scenes and may use more in noisy ones. CBR holds the set bitrate (most detail in busy scenes, largest files). Each video's frame list records the mode used.
Sound is recorded on every phone. The Sound offset (auto) corrects the delay of each phone's audio.
4K at 80 Mbit/s uses about 600 MB per minute. The camera phone shows how many minutes still fit (≈ min video).

With the remote trigger you can take stereo photos or videos with another camera app: Google Camera (e.g. Night Sight or Portrait mode) or Blackmagic Camera (its many video settings). SyncCamPhone switches its own cameras off but keeps the clock sync running in the background. A floating 3D button on the CONTROL phone presses the other app's shutter or record button on all phones at the same moment.

The other app takes the photo or starts the video 0 to 2 frames (0 to about 70 ms) after the press, differently on each phone, and its video frames are not kept in step. Use the remote trigger for still scenes (landscapes, buildings); for moving subjects use SyncCamPhone's own modes.
On every phone: Android Settings → Apps → SyncCamPhone → three-dot menu → Allow restricted settings.
On every phone: Settings → Accessibility → SyncCamPhone → on. The app uses this only to press the button of the camera app while the remote trigger is running.
On the CONTROL phone: allow display over other apps when the app asks (needed for the floating button).
In SyncCamPhone on the CONTROL phone: Settings → SYSTEM → Start remote trigger.
Open the camera app on all phones and choose the same mode and settings.

Wait until the floating 3D button is green, then tap it. All phones press the shutter (or record button) 0.4 s later at the same moment. Drag the 3D button away from the app's own buttons, so that it does not cover them.
To stop: return to SyncCamPhone on the CONTROL phone and press Stop remote trigger. The normal cameras and the sync start again.

The numbers show how many camera phones have a good clock sync, out of all camera phones (a stereo pair shows 1/1 or 0/1; yellow appears only with two or more camera phones). If the button is not green, wait a few seconds; tapping it anyway gives photos that may not be in sync.

Keep the phones level and parallel; the lenses at the same height.
The lens distance of a typical bar (6–7 cm, like human eyes) suits subjects from about 2 m away. For distant landscapes a wider base gives more depth.
Avoid very close objects at the picture edges: they are hard to view in 3D.
For video, avoid fast panning: keep the rig steady or on a tripod.
